newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drafting new proposals to pay U.N. dues.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drafting new proposals to pay U.N. dues.

text.p: The United States, worried about losing influence in the United Nations, is working on new proposals to pay off debts of at least $1 billion to the world body, a senior State Department official said Tuesday.
Princeton Lyman, Acting Assistant Secretary of State for International Organisation Affairs, said several plans were being considered to be put to the new Congress, which takes office in January.

Congress, unhappy about alleged U.N. over-spending and mismanagement of peace-keeping operations, cut down past U.S. contributions, leading to arrears that Washington puts at $1 billion and the United Nations says are about $1.3 billion.
Lyman told a news conference there was "a great deal of resentment and anger" among other U.N. members that the United States, while pressing for reform of the organisation, was its largest debtor.

"More and more countries are saying the U.S. has always been the champion of the sanctity of treaties, of contracts and international obligations, and you the United States are in violation of a treaty, an obligation...We recognise that," he said.

"If we don't deal with this effectively in the next year or so, we're going to find it very difficult to mobilise votes in support of the things we need in the United Nations -- not just in the reform area, not just in the budget area, but in some of the areas of security and disarmament that are so important to us."
The United States "will be coming forward with proposals" to deal with the arrears, he said.
He said no decision had yet been taken on the proposals which were being discussed with the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and would have to go to President Bill Clinton.
Lyman said one option was to go back to Congress with a proposal -- rejected by the legislature last year -- to pay off the arrears over five years.
"We're looking at that as one option, we're looking at other ways of perhaps doing it more quickly, but we haven't reached a conclusion," he said.

Congress is demanding that the U.S. contribution to U.N. peacekeeping operations, which accounts for most of the arrears, should be cut from just over 30 percent to 25 percent. But Lyman said U.N. members wanted to be sure that if the percentage was cut, Washington would then meet its dues.
Kofi Annan, the newly-chosen U.N. secretary-general, said on Monday he would speak to the U.S. Congress if necessary to get Washington to pay its debts.

Lyman expressed confidence in the abilities of Annan, elected by the Security Council last week after the United States vetoed the re-appointment of his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali. Washington said Boutros-Ghali had failed to reform the U.N. bureaucracy quickly enough.
"We have great optimism that (Annan) will be a very forceful, capable leader in the future," he said.

But Lyman said the United Nations faced daunting problems and he conceded that a misleading impression may have been given in the heat of the campaign to unseat Boutros-Ghali that a change of secretary-general would solve everything.
"We have never felt that simply changing the leadership in itself would guarantee reform or would guarantee consensus with the Congress on the future of our contributions," he said.
